question: How does sugar go from an ordinary food to a public-health problem — and who pushes back, with what?
summary: The last half-century reverses the sugar story. Cheap corn sweetener, enabled by the 1973 Farm Bill, replaces cane in American soft drinks; portions grow ('Supersize It!'); fast food, convenience food and children's cereals spread; and sugar is engineered into products by the pursuit of a 'bliss point' ([[o2]], [[te1]], [[e2]], [[ec5]], [[ec3]], [[t3]]). American soft-drink consumption, 0.6 gallons a head in 1889, reaches 54 gallons a head by 1997, while Coca-Cola sells in over 200 countries ([[ec1]], [[x1]]).

The consequences become measurable and then political. Obesity doubles worldwide from 1980 and childhood obesity and dental decay become public concerns, and a series of reports and campaigns turns sugar into an object of regulation: the American Heart Association's limit in 2009, the WHO's in 2015, Public Health England's report and Jamie Oliver's 'next tobacco', Mexico's soda tax in 2014 and Britain's levy of 2016 ([[ec4]], [[l1]], [[l2]], [[t5]], [[o8]], [[t7]], [[e5]], [[o7]], [[o9]]).

The history is also revised: papers from Harvard show that the sugar industry had paid in the 1960s for a review that blamed fat, and Yudkin's 1972 warning, which had been set aside, is read again ([[t8]], [[t1]]). Meanwhile the supply side is reshaped by quite different forces: Brazil turns cane into fuel after the oil shocks, the Soviet collapse halves Cuba's output, the EU ends its sugar quotas in 2017 and Hawaii's last plantations close ([[te3]], [[w1]], [[w2]], [[ec7]], [[o10]], [[ec10]]).

themes.title: Corn sweeteners and the new food system
text: A guaranteed profit for corn growers makes high-fructose corn syrup cheap; Coca-Cola changes its formula; sugar leaves the sugar bowl and enters packaged, microwaveable and fast food, with large companies controlling most of what the world eats.

themes.title: Marketing, taste science and children
text: The 'bliss point', cereals aimed at children, energy drinks that were once convalescent drinks, and advertising that is largely for low-nutrition foods show how the demand was made.

themes.title: Evidence, warnings and reversal
text: Yudkin and Duffy's books of the 1970s; the obesity statistics; the dental report; Public Health England; the Harvard papers that showed the industry paid for the 1967 review. Each marks a step from a minority warning to a mainstream claim.

themes.title: Regulation and its limits
text: Bans on artificial sweeteners, the end of America's sugar quotas, the WTO's failure to end farm subsidies, soda taxes in Mexico and Britain, WHO limits. Regulation is repeatedly shaped by industry, by public pressure and by what the previous generation's regulation did.

themes.title: Cane after the old empires
text: Cane survives as fuel in Brazil and as the livelihood of poor migrant workers, loses its markets in Cuba, is protected in Europe and the United States, and nearly vanishes from Hawaii.

turning_points.text: The Farm Bill makes high-fructose corn syrup cheap by guaranteeing corn growers a profit.
Brazil launches Proálcool, making sugar an energy crop.
Coca-Cola switches its main drink from cane sugar to corn syrup.
The Soviet collapse removes the main buyer of Cuban sugar.
The American Heart Association sets a daily limit on added sugar.
Mexico's tax on sugar-sweetened drinks: purchases of taxed drinks fall.
The WHO recommends cutting free sugars to under 10 per cent of energy; Public Health England publishes its report.
Papers show the sugar industry paid for the 1967 review; Britain announces its Soft Drinks Industry Levy.

how_to_read: Unlike earlier folios, nothing here is contested: every entry is a secondary account and the folio's weakness is that it follows one narrative, that of a popular historian of sugar. Treat the folio as the story of how the *argument* about sugar was made and fought, and read *Thought* and *Order* together.
The *Lives* lane carries the health outcomes; *Economy* the volume; and the Nexus the connection from corn subsidies and marketing through to the campaigns of 2015–2016.

The *picture by region* counts the 45 entries: Europe 15, Near East 1, Americas 23, Oceania 1, Worldwide 5; none in Far East or Africa. The story is told from Washington and Britain; Asia and Africa have no entry.

sources.intro: This folio is the most recent and the least tested: all of its entries are secondary, and almost all rest on two popular histories. It should be read as an editorial account of the sugar debate, not as a neutral audit of it.
main: Walvin, *Sugar: The World Corrupted* (about thirty-three entries), a popular history with a clear point of view against the modern sugar industry.
Smith, *Sugar: A Global History*, for the corporate and Hawaiian stories (about twelve); Yudkin, *Pure, White and Deadly*, for the 1970s argument.
contested: The strongest claims, such as the 1960s review paid for by the sugar industry and the comparison to tobacco, are reported by Walvin from news and journalism ([[t8]], [[e5]]).
Causal claims about obesity and sugar taxes are summarised, not tested ([[t6]], [[o7]]).
gaps: No primary scientific or regulatory documents were read; the WHO, PHE and AHA reports are cited secondhand.
The WTO sugar dispute of 2004–05, the sugar industry's own history and the experience of cane-growing countries today are not covered; a global-south source would balance the Anglo-American focus.

text: Fifteen entries: the WTO and the end of EU quotas, the WHO’s 10 per cent limit, Britain’s levy, Jamie Oliver, Yudkin’s *Pure, White and Deadly*, Public Health England and the *Lancet*, soft-drink volumes, children’s teeth and weight, and sugar taxes spreading from Hungary ([[o5]], [[o10]], [[o8]], [[o9]], [[e5]], [[t1]], [[t7]], [[t6]], [[ec8]], [[l1]], [[l2]], [[x2]], [[e3]], [[e4]], [[e1]]).
One entry: Egypt’s republic subsidises sugar with bread and fuel ([[o11]]).
No entry in this folio. Cane and sugar in China, India and Southeast Asia since 1970 are not covered here.

Twenty-three entries, mostly the United States: the cyclamate ban, the Farm Bill and corn syrup, the end of the quota system, saccharin, McDonald’s and cereal, the bliss point, *Liquid Candy*, the AHA limits and the 2016 papers on the sugar industry’s 1960s strategy; Mexico’s tax; Brazil’s Proálcool; and Cuba after the Soviet market ([[o3]], [[o2]], [[te1]], [[o1]], [[o4]], [[e2]], [[ec3]], [[t3]], [[t4]], [[t5]], [[t8]], [[o7]], [[te3]], [[w2]], [[ec7]]).
One entry: Hawaii has one cane grower left in 2015 ([[ec10]]).

Five entries: an estimated two billion overweight people, Coca-Cola in over 200 countries and its bottled-water move, Nestlé’s revenue, and the oil shocks that turn Brazil’s cane into fuel ([[ec4]], [[x1]], [[ec9]], [[ec6]], [[w1]]).
